I would suggest a VM for the one windows program. You can run that VM, with KVM, or even Virtualbox. Here is a guide for KVM that is fairly decent. KVM Guide

I find that Wine tends to take a bit of work to get some things working right. According to WineHQ.org, Revit isnt working in Wine yet. Wine-Revit

Mint is a decent suggestion. Since it is built on Debian / Ubuntu, you can use the Ubuntu answers to many questions. I find the Ubuntu user forums to be quite new user friendly.
I'll get it all set and give KVM a try, revit is pretty CPU intensive hope it runs smoothly in a VM.

I do Openstack for a living. The modern cloud runs on KVM. It should be pretty good. Just look into setting it up properly to assign enough resources. That VM would need the bulk of the system resources.

The Linux environment itself can run in a very small amount of resources.

Virtualbox might be easier and will give you a lot more options up front where you'll see them. Ranked for performance Virtualbox is still faster than xen and there are a lot of big companies that use xen so I wouldn't sweat that kvm is slightly faster than virtualbox. The slowest part of any desktop use of a vm is the graphics buffering. Integration into hardware is the key so that applications inside can take advantage of hardware acceleration and not have to draw to windows, then be draw to linux, then to hardware. Virtualbox has put more effort into getting that more likely to be right in more setups than kvm has.

So
1. Easier
2. Almost equally fast on compute
3. Likely better where you will may actually see a performance loss.
Mint is a decent starting choice for a Linux Distro and you'll find it has drivers for the popular Virtual Machines like VirtualBox pre-installed.

Wine is rarely stable enough to run software you use every day. The glitching would drive you mad after a week even if you could get it to work.

Look into VMs with GPU pass through, because Revit looks pretty graphically intensive.

If Revit isn't 100% Wine compatible, and your daily work flow revolves around that one program, my advice, sadly, is to stick with windows.
